en: The *Candrāloka*, composed by the poet Śrī Jayadeva, who showers forth the splendor of nectar.

May the Goddess of Speech shine forth, who—like the three eyes of the Wielder of the Axe—is radiant in the mind, banishing the dullness of the lotus, dispelling the darkness of the moon with her manifest stains, and surpassing the blossoming flowers; she who is the pure flame of the rising, bold Destroyer of Desire (Śiva) and the revealer of the three worlds.
Ha! Ho! O moons of the mind consisting of pure consciousness, increase the aesthetic flavors! O you wanton and thoughtless poetry, do not manifest before us!
The virtuous one, raining nectar, himself spreads forth this moonlight for the delight of the ocean of waters adorned with the multitude of waves of discernment. 1.2.

O wise ones, let this ocean of Sarasvatī—the essence of literature—be resorted to as your refuge; it possesses unfathomable depth and is the sole abode of the languid nectar to be savored through reasoning.

From this [ocean] comes prosperity consisting of skill in instruction; from this comes the ambrosia for the world; from this comes the moon of fame, whose filaments are the blossoming lotuses of radiant states.
We praise that rising mass of light— the words of the Sun-like former masters—
by proclaiming which my own virtues shine forth like motes of dust in a sunbeam.
One should not suspect that their doctrine is being refuted by this;
rather, it is adorned, like the eyes of gazelle-eyed women with collyrium.
Inspiration itself, when accompanied by the practice of hearing [the scriptures], is the cause for poetry,
just as a string of seeds bound together by clay and water is the cause for a creeper.
Speech that is faultless, possessing the [poetic] characteristics, adorned with merits,
endowed with ornaments and various sentiments, and exhibiting manifold styles, bears the name of "kāvya."
Why does that skilled person who accepts that poetry consists of word and meaning without ornament not likewise accept fire as being non-hot? 1.8.
A word that is etymologically derived and suitable for the production of case-endings is accepted as being technical (*śāstrīya*).
Furthermore, it is divided into three types by way of its sub-varieties: conventional (*rūḍha*), etymological (*yaugika*), and mixed (*tanmiśra*). (JCand 1.9)
The first [type of yoga] is threefold: the unmanifest (avyakta), the yoga-departure (niryoga), and the semblance of yoga (yogābhāsa);
these correspond respectively to the tree and so forth, the earth and so forth, and the pavilion and so forth.
The etymological [meaning] is threefold, through the distinctions of the pure, the root, and the combined;
and these take the forms of Bhrānti, Sphuratkānti, Kaunteya, and so forth.
Intermingled with these through the mutual transformation of general and particular qualities,
there arise the ocean, the lotus, the palace, the sea, the tree, and the moon.
The ocean of milk and the lotus in the sky are established by that;
a word is a form ending in a case-suffix, and a sentence is a collection of such words through the completion of the sense. (JCand 1.13)
And that [sentence], lacking the state of having a logically connected meaning, is held to be a fragmentary sentence;
moreover, a sentence, a fragmentary sentence, and even a single word are [all considered such] in certain cases.

Just as the address "O Devadatta" [is used], so too a collection of sentences that rest upon a single meaning is called a "sentence-cluster" (vākyakadambaka). Thus, for example, [the argument] "because it possesses smoke. 1.15.

May this first ray of the *Candrāloka*, composed by the great poet Jayadeva— whose parents were Mahādeva, uniquely skilled in the science of sacrificial rituals headed by the *sattra* sacrifice, and Sumitrā, whose mind was devoted to his worship— long bring joy to the wise.
They proclaim that defect which, when it enters the mind, causes the beauty [of the composition] to be marred, whether it has manifested in the word or in the meaning. (JCand 2.1)
The syllables may be harsh to the ear, skillful at provoking distress upon hearing;
they may be understood as contrary to grammar and corrupted in their phonetic refinement.
The masculine gender and so forth in words such as *daivata* is not applied [to the object];
however, the employment of verbs such as *han* (to strike) with respect to actions such as going (*gamana*) is indeed incapable [of expressing that meaning].

That lover, with his curly locks, kills—alas!—in the wilderness; for when used in connection with words such as *lohitam* (blood), the word *nihata* (struck down) loses its literal meaning through the application of terms like *śoṇita* (red).
That very word which they call "one that expresses an unintended meaning" is this female monkey, who takes delight in playing upon the tips of the branches of the wonderful tree of poetry.
In the verse beginning with "nirarthakaṃ tuhi," [the word] *tuhi* and so forth have the sole purpose of filling out the meter;
in the verse beginning with "arthe vidadhat," the word *dadhat* and so forth are non-expressive (synonymous).
The sun makes the vault of the sky crimson with its youthful rays;
yet, without the single syllable [of the name], the earth, the mountains, and so forth are like the mere expanse of the sky.
Inappropriate speech is of three kinds, consisting of shame, loathsomeness, or inauspiciousness; how could the wind, which is a means of delight, exist at the destruction of beloved ones?

In this context, that which has two meanings might be considered doubtful, as in "birds go to the river" (where it could mean either the water or the bank). That which is unestablished (*apratīta*) is that which is accessible only through scripture, such as the *vītānumāna* and other [categories].
My mind, resting upon you who possess the splendor of the moon, has dissolved languidly upon my bed;
yet the mention of the forehead, the kneecaps, the hips, the buttocks, and the cheeks is called vulgar.

The rays of the moon are interpretable in meaning, unpleasant due to the excessive extension of their figurative implications, and act as sentries during the vigil that mocks the pearl necklace of the moon. (JCand_2.11)
The speech of one whose meaning is defiled reaches the ladder of the series of meanings; such speech is like the flow of the river that is the wife of the father of Hari’s beloved.
When the injunction is concealed by a compound, the portion to be enjoined remains unclarified;
thus, the side-long glances of lovers enter the heart like arrows.
The phrase "independent" (*aparādhīna*) and so forth is considered to produce a contradiction, as it is connected with something else: "the breasts adorned with a lofty necklace. (JCand_2.14)
They know a discordant syllable to be one that is unsuitable for the intended rasa and other aesthetic elements;
[as in]: "O Aṅgada, you do not know me, Rāvaṇa, who am terrible in battle. (JCand 2.15)
In this [verse], where a *visarga* is struck down or elided, it is thus:
"kusandhiḥ paṭav āgaccha" (a bad seam, O weaver, come! and "visandhir nṛpatī imau" (these two kings with a loose joint).
O large-eyed one, if a metrical fault shines forth even when not explicitly stated,
look at the sky rippling with stars! (JCand_2.17)
The flower of your fame, born from your sword, is insufficient to cover the expanse of the sky;
yet the serpent of your blade bites your enemies excessively.
The speech uttered was redundant; her eyes were as dark as blue lotuses;
with their trunks extended far out, the elephants entered the city in a distorted manner.
With his excellence ever-increasing and his subsequent grace surpassing that which preceded it,
here has arrived he who holds in his hand the thunderbolt of profound resolve.
This vessel of nectar,
which brings joy to the eyes, the cool-rayed moon, the kinsman of the ocean, rises once again after its completion.

We praise Śambhu, whose form consists of half a woman with thighs like the trunk of a plantain tree; who, in playful dances, looks expectantly at the other half of the body while smiling, his own undertaking rendered futile.
If the intended connection were not present, there would be an incongruity of thought;
for by whom was the ocean bound, he whose followers we are—Rāma?
Having seized the prosperity of his enemies, he filled his foes with [the fruits of] their own deeds;
yet this was not a composition where compounds were misplaced, nor was it merely pleasing to the learned.
That which is mixed with mutually distinct sentences and words is indeed that [type of confusion]:
"The night shines with the mouth; the beloved woman gleams with the moon."
O Ornament of the Earth, listen: the cosmic egg, filled with the abundance of your fame, acts like a golden pitcher brimming with water.
Broken sequence (*bhagnaprakrama*) is the failure to carry through the words that have been commenced; it is lack of order (*akrama*), as in:
"O Kṛṣṇa, the deities are worshipped without having first honored you. (JCand 2.27)
When a primary meaning creates a contradiction with a secondary meaning, it constitutes the figure *amatārthāntara*:
"The woman, having cast aside her necklace and pressed her breast against her chest, was embraced by grief. (JCand 2.28)
If the meaning is not developed in the substantive, there is no distinction provided by the qualifier:
"The side-glances of the beloved, possessing the luster of wagtails, enter my heart. (JCand 2.29)

That which is difficult to understand, incapable of clear comprehension, or resembles what is merely verbally expressed, is "contradictory" (vyāhata) if there is a mutual opposition between the meanings of the preceding and following parts. (JCand 2.30)
How can your face, with its thousand petals, be compared to anything?
For where is there a comparison when the moon itself has been rendered redundant?
These three defects— difficult progression, vulgarity, and ambiguity— are respectively [avoided here]:
"O Kṛṣṇa, may I, devoted to You, go either to hell or indeed to heaven."
"Give me one kiss and I will give you my bodice.
Tell me, which should be served: the moon-faced woman or the moon-crested Lord? 2.33.

That which always causes the creeper of one's reputation to tremble through impropriety is considered twofold: that which is contrary to worldly renown and that which is contrary to sacred knowledge. (JC 2.34)
Behold this ketakī flower, its radiance white with the splendor of Kandarpa, placed upon the crest of Śambhu; it bears a resemblance to a digit of the moon.
The general transformation would be a body with the luster of a golden earring;
the specific transformation would be a woman within my mind.
Likewise, through association with the beautiful or through mutual opposition, crows and the virtuous do not distinguish between their own offspring and that of another. (JC 2.37)
O lotus-eyed one, behold the moon-like face of your son;
this Indra among men shall protect your lineage.

One should infer, according to the context, the faults arising from words and meanings— whether they pertain to a single word, a portion thereof, a portion of a sentence, a sentence, or a collection of sentences.
They call him the "goad for the defects" who restrains in three ways a fault that has arisen in his mind and is spreading uncontrollably.
It either spreads the quality of virtue within a fault, or it casts away its status as a fault;
or else, it renders that very fault something that cannot be abandoned.
His face bears the splendor of the moon, marked by the sprout-like tips of his white beard;
here, in this depiction of the sentiment of humor (*hāsya-rasa*), vulgarity has attained the status of a poetic quality (*guṇa*).
How did it come to pass that you, born from the ocean of milk, became marked with a digit [of the moon]?
According to the convention of poets, this contradiction with established knowledge has attained the status of being no fault.
Gaurī held in her heart the God marked by the moon;
here, because of the emergence of *śleṣa* (paronomasia), the word "indeed" (*hi*) is not to be discarded as being meaningless.

May this second ray of the *Candrāloka*, composed by that excellent poet Jayadeva, long bring delight to the wise— the son of Mahādeva, who is uniquely skilled in the science of sacrifices headed by the *sattra* rites, and Sumitrā, whose mind was devoted to his worship.
This collection of syllables consists of few words yet reveals a manifold meaning;
furthermore, this Śauri is followed by Uṣā’s beloved, the heroic [Kṛṣṇa].
Even that which is known as a fault is called a beauty when it is set aside by the praise of virtues;
they vainly revile cyclic existence, wherein the Enemy of Kaṃsa is worshipped.
If discursive thought (*vicāra*) is indeed a conceit that negates the inferred object, then how could the moon be intense, and how could the sun exist at night? (JCand 3.3)
Having abandoned many positions through reasoning, one arrives at the certain determination of a single [truth]:
"This is neither the moon nor the sun; it is the submarine fire rising from the ocean and burning. (JCand 3.4)
This is a denial of well-known causes;
it is a disregard for [the fact that] heroes were not struck down by battle, but rather by the mere twitching of eyebrows.
An etymological explanation (nirukta) may consist of a derivation of a name that is either true or false;
O King, by such conduct, you have become a mine of faults despite your truthfulness.
If the determination [of the relationship] were false, then the probandum and the probans would be non-existent;
[in that case], wear a garland of celestial flowers strung together with threads of moonbeams!
If it is said that success is found among those who are renowned, this is stated for the sake of expressing equality:
"In this world, you two alone are famous—you by your powers, and the ocean by its waters."
If you argue that the specific proof is established through the connection with various other meanings,
then you are some extraordinary cloud indeed, since you rain down gold repeatedly.
If the effect consists in the perception of a result arising from an activity, whether in reality or otherwise,
then this moon rises only to cut away the pride of fair-browed women.
The great seers have declared such abundant characteristics to belong to poetry, just as a king possesses [marks] such as a face radiant like gold. (JCand_3.11)

May this third ray of the *Candrāloka*, composed by that excellent poet Jayadeva— whose parents were Mahādeva, uniquely skilled in the science of sacrificial rituals headed by the *sattra* sacrifice, and Sumitrā, whose mind was devoted to his worship— long bring delight to the wise.
śleṣa (punning) is the description of things that appear to be disconnected as being connected;
it is verbal when the connection is brought about by words of the same kind, providing great pleasure.
We praise Hari, embraced by Śrī— who, like a jealous woman, was terrified when he was made to manifest her slender form by the bristling hairs of his body— though he is in fact infinite.
Since every object situated within [the mind] manifests by itself, like the clarity of water, that is known as *prasāda*. (JCand 4.3)
There is equality through the brevity of syllables, or rather, equality through the phonemes and so forth;
the dark-complexioned, tender young woman has gone for refuge to her lover.
Concentration is the greatness of the goal; by means of it, entering within with its nature of shimmering, dense essence, the limbs of the virtuous become sprouted.
Moreover, the sweetness of repetition brings a charm of variety;
friend, look, look at her flickering corner of the eye! (JCand_4.6)
Ojas may be the maturity of meaning or the condensation of what is excessive:
"Having slain the enemy and achieved glory, your sword has entered its sheath. (JCand 4.7)
Through the transformation of its synonyms, gentleness and lack of harshness reached their culmination when he embraced the friend of the wind (Agni) until only his story remained.
Elegance, however, is considered distinct from wit because of its lack of vulgarity:
"O beloved, abandon your pride; raise your eye-corner slightly."
In the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) and in serenity (*prasāda*), there is a collection of clarity of meaning and lucidity;
these ten qualities in poetry are like the virtues of heroism and so forth in a man.
Just as the *tilaka* mark and other ornaments are pleasing to the hearts of clever women,
so too is an ornament distinct from the [original] nature itself the true embellishment of words.
The diverse characteristics, the deployment, the consummation, the propriety, the statement of the secret of other treatises, and the compendium—thus has the direction been shown. (JCand 4.12)

May this fourth ray of the *Candrāloka*, composed by the excellent poet Jayadeva, long bring delight to the wise— the son of Mahādeva, who is uniquely skilled in the science of sacrifices headed by the *sattra*, and Sumitrā, whose mind was devoted to his worship.

Whether through the conventional renown of word and meaning, or by virtue of the poet’s creative mastery, the arrangement that is captivating is an *alaṅkāra* (ornament), like a necklace and so forth. (JCand 5.1)
It possesses the longing for the abundant array of vowels and consonants;
it is the cow that causes the world to awaken from its arrogance, resplendent with clever alliteration.
Speech that is complete with a full range of phonemes, possessing rhythmic alliteration (vṛttyanuprāsa),
is the abode and temple for the free play of a mass of intense bliss.
Where there is the repetition of words with distinct intentions arising from alliteration (lāṭānuprāsa), it is a victory, a victory indeed; for there, the roar of the enemy has not been heard again.

If the repetition of syllables occurs with certainty in half a verse, or even in a quarter of it, then that is considered by the wise to be "clear alliteration" (sphuṭānuprāsa) according to the virtuous.
Alliteration of meaning (arthānuprāsa) is desired in cases such as the comparison of the object compared to the standard of comparison; for instance:
"The sandalwood [is indeed] the salutation of the pair of feet of Govinda."
Making the edge of his garment appear like a taut repetition and resembling a redundant meaning, this moon approaches the edge of the sky.

Those whose speech possesses the sweetness of the foremost masters know *yamaka*— which has clusters of repeated syllables and is the sprout from the bulbous root of praise— to be the first [ornament] of poetry.
Among the various marvelous forms such as the *khaḍgabandha* (sword-arrangement) and others observed by the most eminent connoisseurs of poetry,
the first is said to be this pair of verses that delights the virtuous.
Like a passionate woman, the line of the sword shall be beautiful and terrifying;
with limbs reddened by the application of saffron, it clings to the necks of enemies.
An *upamā* (simile) is that wherein the splendor of similarity between two things shines forth,
as when [the beauty] plays intensely in the heart, like the breasts of a slender-limbed woman.
When a single entity alone functions as both the standard of comparison and the object of comparison—
as in "the moon is like the moon" and so forth— there occurs the figure known as *ananvaya* (non-correspondence).
If that same [quality] is expressed through a reciprocal exchange between two things, it is considered "the comparison of the compared" (upameyopamā):
"In you, Dharma is like Artha in its full splendor, and Artha is like Dharma. (JCand_5.13)
When that which is well-known as a standard of comparison becomes the object of comparison—
as in "the face is like the moon" and so forth— that is then the *pratīpopamā* (inverse simile).
But when the object of comparison is enriched with words such as "playfulness" (līlā) and the like, it is the *lalitopamā* (graceful simile):
"Your pair of eyes bears the playfulness of blue lotuses."
The simile of a cluster (stabakopamā) consists in the similarity between multiple pairs of objects:
"I have taken refuge at the feet of Viṣṇu, just as a bee [takes refuge] at a lotus."
There may be a complete simile (*saṃpūrṇopamā*) where both [the subject and the object] are predicated, as in:
"At the break of day, the eyes were like lotuses blossoming. (JCand_5.17)
Wherever the wall consisting of the object of comparison is entirely colored by the image of the standard of comparison, there *rūpaka* (metaphorical identification) is desired.
The metaphorical figure *sopādhi-rūpaka* (metaphor with a qualifying condition) arises from the superimposition of a property to be proven upon that which possesses a common attribute:
"He is the Indra who shatters the wings of the visible haughty mountains."
When a visible object is described as being similar to something else that has been mentioned separately, it is a "metaphor of similarity" (sādṛśyarūpaka).
"Your tree-like arm, with its five shining branches [fingers], shines forth."
"May there be a slender body"—such is a metaphorical metaphor (*ābhāsa-rūpaka*);
"the vine of the bow of her slender body," and so forth, is a metaphor of a metaphor (*rūpita-rūpaka*).
In that transformation in which the non-difference of these two culminates,
she, when questioned by her beloved in secret, gave silence alone as her answer.
The description of a single object in many ways by many people is considered "multiple description" (ullekha).
He was perceived as the God of Love by women, as the moon by those dear to him, and as Death by his enemies.
Apahnuti (concealment) consists in the denial of a reality in order to superimpose something unreal:
"This is not the moon; what then? It is a lotus in the celestial Ganges. (JC 5.24)
Paryastāpahnuti (disguised denial) occurs where the property alone is denied:
"This is not the moon; what then? It is the face of my beloved."
When one thing is determined to be real through the suspicion of another, there occurs a "denial by delusion" (bhrāntāpahnuti).
O friend, does not love cause a fever that spreads a burning heat accompanied by trembling? (JCand_5.26)
Chekāpahnuti (Artful Denial) occurs when there is a denial of a fact due to a suspicion of something else:
"Is it not my beloved’s anklet that is clinging to my foot as he speaks? (5.27)
*kaitavāpahnuti* (disguised denial) occurs when there is a concealment through words such as "pretext" (*vyāja*) once [the fact] is revealed:
"The arrows of Smara are emerging under the pretext of the glances cast by my beloved. (JC 5.28)
Where a cause or other factor is suggested through poetic fancy (utprekṣā) without concealment:
"Surely the moon acts as an enemy to the lotuses for the sake of the beauty of your face. (JCand_5.29)
In the absence of words such as "iva" and so forth, they call this *gūḍhotprekṣā* (concealed fancy), as in:
"His fame, weary from wandering, entered the river of heaven."
Through memory, error, and doubt, that very same triad of ornaments may occur:
"As I gaze upon the lotus, my mind plunges into her face. (JCand 5.31)
This intoxicated bee knows whether your face is a lotus or the moon; as for us, however, there is no certainty.
If, due to great similarity, a closed eye is not perceived as distinct [from its object],
then the red lac was not perceived on her foot, which was naturally crimson.
If a universal were not perceived as distinct from similarity,
then the faces of the fair-browed women who had entered the lotus pond would not have been distinguished.
Due to some particularity of the cause, a manifestation is considered to be "unveiled," just as when the moon has risen, both the lotuses and the faces are observed [to bloom]. (JCand 5.35)
And inference is the ascertainment of a cause from its effect and so forth;
there exists some [cause] by which, having seen me, she has smiled slightly.
Presumption (arthāpatti) would be established by itself through the description of other objects:
the moon is already defeated by your face—what then can be said of the lotuses?
Or there may be *kāvyaliṅga* (poetic figure of causal indication), where word and meaning support a novel sense:
"O dull-witted Kandarpa, you are conquered; for the Three-eyed Lord dwells within my heart. (JCand_5.38)
The figure of speech *parikara* consists of an adjective possessing intentional meaning (*sābhiprāya*).
May Śiva, who wears the moon as his crest-ornament, remove your suffering. (JCand 5.39)
But when the substantive possesses an underlying intention (*sābhiprāya*), it becomes a "germinating ornament" (*parikarāṅkura*):
"The four-armed God is the bestower of the four aims of human life. (JCand 5.40)
If this is a case of "simultaneous hyperbole" (*akramātiśayokti*) regarding cause and effect occurring at once:
O Lord, your arrows and your enemies alike embrace the bowstring together.
Extreme hyperbole (*atyantātiśayokti*) occurs when there is a reversal of their sequence:
"O beloved, her pride departed first, and afterwards she was conciliated by him. (JCand 5.42)
The hyperbole of excess (capalātiśayokti), however, occurs when the effect arises from the application of the cause:
"When she was asked by her beloved, 'Are you coming?', her bracelets became rings. (JCand 5.43)
The poetic figure *sambandhātiśayokti* (hyperbole of relation) occurs when there is a statement of a relation even in its absence;
for example: "Behold, the orb of the moon shines, clinging to the top of the palace."
If an exaggeration of distinction (*bhedakātiśayokti*) consists in describing one thing as something else entirely, [an example is]:
"Oh, how truly unique is the play of beauty upon the surface of the young girl's breasts! (JCand 5.45)
If there is an excellence of metaphorical identification (*rūpakātiśayokti*), then that which is identified is situated within the metaphor itself:
"Behold, from the pair of blue lotuses, sharp arrows emerge! (JCand 5.46)
Bold assertion (*prauḍhokti*) is the imagining of something as capable when it is actually incapable; for example:
"The dark, straight-growing trees on the banks of the Yamunā."
If such a possibility were to exist—that is, if there were a conjecture for the sake of establishing another fact:
"If pearls, moistened by waters turned white by their staying within crystal jars, should produce a creeper with flowers equal to your fame... JCand_5.48 //
The attainment of more than what was desired without effort is *praharṣaṇa* (the delightful).
One should illuminate the lamp only so long as the sun has not yet risen.
But despair is the attainment of a result contrary to what was desired;
as long as one might light a lamp, it is already extinguished.
*Tuḷyayogitā* (Equal Pairing) is the equality of many things through action and so forth:
"The lotuses contract, as do the faces of wanton women, when the moon, its orb kissing the peak of the eastern mountain, has risen. (JCand_5.51)
When there is equality between the subject at hand and that which is not, it is considered *dīpaka* (the illuminator):
"The wise man bears wisdom; the moon bears nectar; and you bear the earth."
When the word *dīpaka* (illuminator) is repeated, it becomes *āvṛttidīpaka* (repeated illuminator):
"The fire shines with its flame; the moon shines with its splendor; the sun shines with its radiance."
When there is a commonality of meaning between two sentences, it is considered a *prativastūpamā* (simile by parallelism), as in:
"The sun shines with its heat, and the hero shines with his bow."
If the state of being an original object and its reflection were the example, it would be a poetic ornament;
if it were the state of being a wrestler and his opponent, it would be the loud roar at the height of battle.
If your form is the example [of beauty], then the cruel writing of fate has been polished;
for if the radiance of the sun has arisen, then the night has departed.
*Nidarśanā* is the superimposition of identity between two similar sentence-meanings:
"That gentleness of the donor is this very spotlessness of the moon. (JC 5.57)
If there is a distinction (*vyatireka*) between the object of comparison and the subject of comparison, as in:
"The virtuous are lofty like mountains, yet they are naturally gentle," [this is a case of *vyatireka*].
Co-utterance (sahokti) occurs when a simultaneous occurrence shines forth, delighting the people:
"His fame went to the ends of the earth along with his enemies."
If *vinokti* is defined as stating that the subject under discussion is deficient without something else, [then it would apply here]:
"Learning, though pleasing to the heart, is blameworthy without the perfection of discipline. (JCand 5.60)
Samāsokti (synecdoche) occurs when there is a vivid manifestation of the unmentioned [subject] within the mentioned;
for example: "Behold this face of Indra! The red moon kisses it."
If there is a pun consisting of word-splitting (*khaṇḍaśleṣa*), where each [part] has a separate meaning:
"The lord of the army shone, with abundant blood gushing forth. (JCand_5.62)
If the punning dissolution of a collection of words implies a distinct meaning for each part,
then for whom would the city of Ayodhyā not be as dear as immortality?
Arthaśleṣa (semantic paronomasia) occurs when a single word has recourse to multiple meanings; for example:
"Your side-long glances and your curls are both crooked, dark, and long."
Aprastutapraśaṃsā (Indirect Description) occurs where that which is described follows upon what is relevant;
it is considered to consist of the relation between cause and effect, the general and the particular, and so forth.
What beautiful thing has not been obtained by means of lotuses, the abodes of Lakṣmī?
Even those who possess perseverance reach the far shore of the ocean.
Arthāntaranyāsa (corroboration by another matter) occurs when there is the statement of a related secondary meaning:
"Hanumān crossed the ocean; what is difficult for the great-souled?"
That [state] in which particularities and generalities are distinguished is the "expanding" [samādhi];
it was not conquered, for the great are as unassailable as mountains.
They declare *paryāyokti* (periphrasis) to be that which is expressed through matters such as effects (*kārya*) that have been introduced; [as in]:
"He caused grass to sprout in the palaces of the enemy kings. (JCand 5.69)
Indirect praise (*vyājastuti*) consists of praise through censure or censure through praise; for example:
"What is your discernment, since you lead even sinners to heaven? (JCand_5.70).
Rebuttal, however, is the denial of what has been asserted through investigation:
"Show yourself, O Moon, or else there exists the face of my beloved. (JCand 5.71)
A "hidden objection" (gūḍhākṣepa) occurs when an injunction is explicit while a prohibition is unclear:
"Take Sītā happily; however, [consider] the arrival of Death."
If you claim that there is a contradiction because [the word "intoxication"] cannot logically apply to qualities, substances, actions, and so forth,
then let the intense flow of sandalwood juice burn me at its own will.
If there is a contradiction arising from such devices as *śleṣa* (paronomasia) and the like, it is considered "apparent contradiction" (*virodhābhāsa*).
"Even though this world is shrouded in darkness by him, it is illuminated."
The impossibility of accomplishing an objective is described as its inconceivability:
"Who knows? Will a cowherd boy uproot a mountain? (JCand 5.75)
If an effect could arise even without a cause through mere destruction,
look at your two feet, which have become red from being sprinkled with lac-dye.
Viśeṣokti (the figure of speech of "peculiar cause") is the non-arising of an effect despite the presence of its cause:
"No one at all transgresses against a wise man, even when he bows down. (JCand 5.77)
If [the two terms] are stated as being in different locations, there is an incongruity between the effect and the cause:
"The limbs of your devotees bow down, while the exhaustion of worldly existence goes to ruin. (Jñānaśrīmitra’s *Cintāmaṇi*, 5.78)
If the assumption of multiple connections is considered improper due to inconsistency,
then where are the snakes with such virulent poison, and where is this sandalwood tree?
The description of the connection between multiple objects according to propriety is *samam*; for example:
"The breast-mound was made a fitting abode by the necklace. (JCand 5.80)
If effort were to yield diverse results, it would bestow even contrary fruits;
yet the virtuous bow down even to obtain exaltation from the three worlds.
The description of the qualities of the supported as exceeding those of the support is called *adhikam* (the hyperbolic).
Your virtues do not find room within that speech by which the entire world is pervaded.
Mutuality is that wherein there is mutual assistance;
the night shines by means of the moon, and the moon shines by means of the night.
A particular type of *khyāta* is the description of the supported even without the support:
"Even when the sun has set, the rays of the lamp situated within dispel the darkness."
There would be a contradiction if one thing were said to act in a way other than it actually does;
for by those very things by which the world is delighted, the flower-weaponed god [Kāma] destroys it.
The *kāraṇamālā* (garland of causes) is a *gumpha* (interlocking composition) consisting of causes arranged from the preceding to the following, as in:
"Through policy comes prosperity; through prosperity, generosity; and through generosity, vast fame."
A single string (*ekāvalī*) is considered to be a series of meanings arranged according to the manner of being grasped and released:
"The eyes rest at the ends of the ears; the ears dangle down to the roots of the arms. (JCand_5.87)
Through the combination of the *dīpaka* (illuminator) and the *ekāvalī* (single-string necklace), it is called *mālādīpaka* (garland-illuminator):
"By Smara [the god of love], she was placed in his heart; by him, she was established in you."
"Sāra" (essence) refers to the excellence of words, which increases in its essentiality further and further;
therein lies the essence of Sarasvatī, therein poetry, and therein the hymn to Śiva.
If a quality of noble essence shines forth as distinct yet appearing non-distinct,
then that is sweet honey, nectar, and therefore the speech of a poet.
If the two meanings correspond respectively, they are joined one by one in sequence:
"Conquer the enemy, delight the friend, and crush the faction of the foe. (JCand 5.91)
If a synonym were to apply to many things, then a single quality could be shared among them;
yet the comparison "resembling the face of a longing woman" departs from the lotus and goes to the moon.
Exchange is the mutual substitution of one thing for another that is inferior or superior;
[as in the case where] he released a single arrow and took in the side-long glances of his enemies' wives.
Exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*) is the restriction of one thing to another by negating the former;
in the case of lamps, there is a depletion of oil, but not so in the hearts of those with arched brows.
Conceptualization is a conflict between two things of equal strength, accompanied by cleverness;
therefore, you should cultivate detachment toward the beloved’s heart or even her lower lip.
The conjunction (*samuccaya*) is the arrangement of many things sharing a single connection:
"Your enemies perish, they see [the end], and they fall. (JCand 5.96)
Concentration arises from the proximity of other causal factors that facilitate the accomplishment of the task;
perceiving her longing, the sun went to its setting.
His prowess was directed against the faction of a powerful enemy;
his ears, following the victorious eyes, surpassed blue lotuses.
The inverse [type of simile] consists in the inferiority of the standard of comparison relative to the object of comparison; for example:
"If her face has been seen, what need is there for a lotus, or for the moon?"
If it is argued that there is joy because of the greatness of another, yet a fault is described elsewhere,
then that is simply the misfortune of wealth, in that it does not take refuge in the virtuous.
The quality of that [lip] arises from the abandonment of its own qualities by the other;
thus, the nose-pearl, though naturally red as a ruby, has taken refuge in your lower lip.
Furthermore, the attainment of one's own inherent qualities should be understood as the "prior form" (*pūrvarūpatā*);
for even though Śeṣa is smeared by the rays from the throat of Hara, he remains white through your fame.
If a thing were to possess a different form [than its own], it would likewise possess its former form;
for when a lamp has been extinguished, the splendor of the day would have existed [within its jewels].
They call "atadguṇa" (the non-acceptance of another's qualities) the failure to acknowledge virtues that have been joined [to oneself].
Even though it enters into the midst of the sun, the moon always remains cold.
The excellence of her own qualities, already established from before, is enhanced by the proximity of another;
thus, even with her sidelong glances, she turns the blue lotuses of her ears into the very color of her eyes.
If an object is described as being contemptible because it is incapable of discerning virtues or faults,
what loss is there to the moon if its lotuses wither?
When questions and answers are stated in succession, it is called *uttarottara* (the "answer-and-answer" figure), as in:
"O traveler, where that cane tree is, there that river flows most abundantly."
The behavior of another who knows the affairs of others is concealed;
when her lover returned home in the morning, the beloved prepared the bed.
*Vyājokti* (disguised speech) is the concealment of a fact by means of a pretext on the part of one who is apprehensive:
"Friend, look, I am grey with the pollen from the garden of the house. (JCand 5.109)
*Vakrokti* (indirect speech) is the imagining of another meaning for the expressed sense through either punning (*śleṣa*) or intonation (*kāku*).
"Abandon your pride! The day has arrived; O dull-witted one, rejoice in the presence of Hara! *JCand_5.110*
Svābhāvokti (Natural Description) is the description of an inherent nature, as well as [the description] of birth and so forth:
"O lady with surging waves for eyes, the deer gaze up at you with ears pricked. (JCand 5.111)
The *bhāvika* [figure of speech] is the description of the direct perception of past and future events;
look well enough at this, for even now the gods and asuras continue to fight here! (JCand 5.112)
The vision of one who is separated by space and self is but a semblance of reality;
yet you, dwelling in her heart, are seen as the five-arrowed god himself in person.
The life of that mountain was noble, praiseworthy, and a model for others;
on its peak occurred the battle between Dhūrjaṭi and the wearer of the crown (Śiva and Arjuna).
Exaggeration (*atyukti*) is the description of marvelous, yet unreal, qualities such as heroism, magnanimity, and so forth.
"O Indra among kings, when you are the giver, even beggars are like the wish-fulfilling trees. (JCand 5.115)
Based on rasa, bhāva, their semblances (tadābhāsa), and the pacification of emotion (bhāvaśānti),
there are those designated as *rasavat*, *preyas*, *ūrjasvin*, and *samāhita*.
Some wise scholars have stated that there are seven ornaments: the arising of entities, conjunction, and variegation—these three; [along with] the remaining four. JCand_5.117
Purity, singleness of purpose, as well as commingling and confusion—these are merely arrangements of these very [figures], and they are not distinct ornaments. (JCand 5.118)
And for all those who bear the distinctions of opposites and counter-images,
some limiting condition (upādhi) may manifest in one place, because it is possible elsewhere as well.
And this succession of garlands of these many [flowers] comes to serve as an ornament upon some man who is favorable to you. (JC 5.120)
Whether in the meaning of a word, the meaning of a sentence, or in a cluster of sentence-meanings,
these arrangements exist as consisting of natural excellence.

Because they are defined by the mention of some excellence (*atiśaya*), as seen from an etymological investigation, these figures of speech (*alaṃkāra*) are for the most part not distinct from hyperbole (*atiśayokti*). (JCand 5.122)
Even when they possess equality in their preeminence of ornamentation,
a distinct difference appears in each individual, just as it does among faces.
If the wise have no regard for ornaments that are [merely] conventional, then let the tradition of names be sought among the more recent varieties of names.

May this fourth ray of the *Candrāloka*, composed by the great poet Jayadeva, long bring joy to the wise— the son whose parents were Mahādeva, uniquely skilled in the science of sacrifices headed by the *sattra* rite, and Sumitrā, whose mind was devoted to his worship.
The determinants (vibhāva) consist of the objective basis (ālambana) and the excitant (uddīpana); the effect is twofold:
the consequents (anubhāva) and the transitory states (bhāva); and there is also the auxiliary, namely the evanescent emotions (vyabhicārin).
In the hearts of those whose nature is not insentient, the emergence of another object of experience that is dissolving brings about a joy that blossoms like the application of sandalwood paste.

In poetry, drama, and dramatic performance, the stable emotion (sthāyibhāva), when manifested by the determinants (vibhāva) and other factors, and existing as a single essence being relished, is known as aesthetic flavor (rasa).
Consisting of the permanent emotional state (sthāyibhāva) called love (rati), it is manifested by excitants such as a beloved woman,
and is accompanied by transitory emotions (saṃcārins) excluding indolence, jealousy, and disgust.

The erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra) is considered to be of two kinds: union (sambhoga) and separation (vipralambha), characterized respectively by the ancillary emotions (anubhāva) such as side-long glances and the like, and by states such as madness and the like.

The comic rasa (hāsya) has laughter as its dominant emotion (sthāyibhāva), and it is accompanied by determinants (vibhāvas) such as deformity, bloated cheeks, and dissimulation (avahitthā), respectively.

The *karuṇa* (compassionate) rasa arises when the stable emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) of grief is combined with its determinants (*vibhāva*) and other factors, such as the gradual exhaustion caused by the falling of tears from separation from the beloved.
The Furious sentiment (raudra-rasa), which has anger as its stable emotion (sthāyibhāva),
is endowed with determinants (vibhāva) and other factors such as envy, the clenching of fists, and delusion, respectively.

The heroic sentiment (*vīra*) has the stable emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) called enthusiasm (*utsāha*), which arises from determinants (*vibhāva*) such as power; it is accompanied by consequents (*anubhāva*) such as steadfastness and by transitory emotions (*bhāva*) such as pride.

The *bhayānaka* (the terrifying) has fear as its stable emotion (*sthāyibhāva*), characterized by excitants (*vibhāva*) such as tigers and the like, accompanied by ensuants (*anubhāva*) such as trembling, and associated with transitory emotions (*vyabhicāribhāva*) such as delusion.

The permanent emotion (sthāyin) of the loathsome (bībhatsa) rasa is disgust; its determinants (vibhāvas) and other factors are, in their respective order, considered to be the sight of the undesirable, spitting, fainting, and so forth.
This marvelous [rasa] has wonder as its stable emotion (sthāyibhāva), arises from excitants such as magic (vibhāva),
has physical manifestations such as horripilation as its ensuants (anubhāva), and has paralysis and so forth as its transitory emotions (vyabhicāribhāva).
The *śānta* (quiescent) rasa has detachment as its dominant emotion (*sthāyibhāva*), arises from excitants (*vibhāva*) such as association with the virtuous,
has patience and so forth as its ensuants (*anubhāva*), and possesses paralysis (*stambha*) and other transitory states (*vyabhicāribhāva*).
Love directed toward objects such as the gods and so forth, as well as the transitory emotions (vyabhicāribhāvas),
when being experienced, are designated as "emotions" (bhāvas) by those learned in literary aesthetics.
Disgust, languor, and doubt; likewise envy, intoxication, and fatigue; as well as indolence, dejection, anxiety, delusion, memory, and fortitude.
Shame, fickleness, joy, agitation, as well as dullness, pride, despondency, longing, sleep, and epilepsy; JCand_6.16 //
Sleep, awakening, indignation, dissimulation, and ferocity; likewise, mental confusion, disease, madness, and even death.
Terror and deliberation are also to be known as transitory emotions;
these thirty-three states have thus been fully enumerated by name.
When love, humility, and so forth are directed toward common objects,
they are declared to be *rasābhāsa* (semblances of rasa) and *bhāvābhāsa* (semblances of emotion), due to their impropriety.
The quiescence, emergence, transition,
and variegation of emotion serve to enhance the beauty of poetry, just as saffron enhances the luster of gold.
There may be a compound with words up to the seventh [from the end] as desired, starting from the eighth;
however, there should never be a compound [of more than seven].
The Pāñcālikī, Lāṭīyā, Gauḍīyā,
and Vaidarbhī are known as the four styles (rītis), corresponding respectively to the aesthetic sentiments (rasas).

In the Madhurā meter, the syllables belonging to their respective groups are occupied by their own fifth [consonants], as is the letter *la* joined with *la*; furthermore, the letters *ra* and *ṇa* are separated by short vowels.

The gutturals (ka-varga), palatals (ca-varga), and retroflexes (ṭa-varga)—excluding the fifth letter of the retroflex group—along with the dentals (ta-varga) preceded by the letter 'ra', and the head of the letter 'ka' (the visarga), occur in the *prauḍhā* [vīṇā]. (JCand 6.24)
In all cases, the *s* is [replaced] by all the upward-pointing [consonants], and the *r* by all [the consonants] in every way;
however, in the *paruṣā* meter, the *ra* and *ha* are joined in two ways, while *ś* and *ṣ* occur naturally.
The letter *la* uncombined with others, the light syllables, and the *gha*, *bha*, *dha*, and *ra* syllables—these are the *vṛttis* in the Lalitā meter;
likewise, the remaining ones are in the Bhadrā meter. Thus are the *vṛttis*.
The graceful play of a young woman, radiant with the movement of her limbs, serves as an archway for the God of Love;
it is in vain for those whose intellects are sharpened by the harshness of logical argumentation.
The peacock, his beak moistened by repeatedly darting forward, was overcome by thirst;
the female crane, however, maintained her impetuousness amidst the increasingly dense mass of clouds.

May that sixth [chapter], composed by the great poet Jayadeva, bring long-lasting joy to the *Candrāloka*, which was created by him whose parents were Mahādeva—unique in his mastery of the science of sacrificial rituals headed by the *sattra* sacrifice—and Sumitrā, whose mind was devoted to his worship; and who is like a ray of light. 6.29.
Endowed with three distinct modes of expression like the Ganges with its various streams,
the profound speech of the Buddha shines forth— sometimes winding and sometimes straight.
The operation consisting of suggestion (*vyañjanā*) belongs to speech that clearly intends another meaning while manifesting its own; it is like the sidelong glance of a woman with tremulous eyes.
There are two varieties of that in which the expressed meaning is not intended to be primary (avivakṣitavācya):
when the expressed meaning itself is either transferred into another meaning (saṃkramita) or completely set aside (atyantatiraskṛta).

Of the type where the expressed meaning is intended to be conveyed (vivakṣitavācya), there are two kinds—those in which the sequence [of suggestion] is manifest (lakṣyakrama) and those in which it is unmanifest (alakṣyakrama).
Of these two, there are respectively forty-one and six varieties.
It arises clearly from the power of the word, the meaning, and their combination in three ways;
however, it arises without a clear sequence primarily through rasa, bhāva, and their semblances (tadābhāsa).
There are two varieties of manifestation arising from the power of words (*śabdaśakti*) concerning both matter (*vastu*) and ornament (*alaṅkāra*).
There are twelve varieties of that which arises from the power of meaning (*arthaśakti*), as follows: [JCand_7.6]
There are four types: the ornament reveals the subject, the subject reveals the ornament, the ornament reveals the ornament, and the subject reveals the subject. (JCand_7.7)

The suggestive meaning is produced by the maturity of either the speaker or the poet composed by the poet, or it is self-established; thus, from these [two], there are four [types of suggestion], each being threefold.
That one [power] arises from both word and meaning, and it rests solely upon the sentence;
it is also present in parts of words, in composition, in phonemes, and in sentences and words.
And in the case of a literary composition (*prabandha*), this [suggestion] called "rasa" and so forth is sixfold and has an indistinct sequence (*asphuṭakrama*).
Among these seventeen [types], one should exclude that single type which has an indistinct sequence.
Those sixteen [types of suggestion] and the others, when doubled, become thirty-two based on the support of sentences and words;
furthermore, there would be twelve varieties arising from the power of meaning even within a continuous composition.
There are thirty-two, twelve, one, and six varieties of the combined sound;
thus there are fifty-one distinct types, yet when intermingled, they become thousands.
The suggested meaning (vyaṅgya), which is intended by the speaker, is woven into the speaker's [utterance];
though not identical in form to it, it has sprouted from its own [source] and blossoms spontaneously through speech.
Some are common [to all], some are awakened by being addressed,
some are bystanders, and some are awakened by one who has already been awakened.
Thus, due to the diversity of perceivers, that which is woven by the speaker is considered fourfold;
and through indifference and concealment, it is held to be twofold when it has sprouted within oneself.
Through the distinctions of the elements and time, there are manifold denials;
by this differentiation as well, the creeper of manifestation flourishes.
When, through various distinctions determined in certain contexts and so forth,
one word expresses another meaning, that is held to be the expressed (vācya) and the suggested (vyaṅgya).
May that Great God (Mahādeva), who alone is expert in the science of sacrifices headed by the Sattra, and whose parents were Sumitra— whose mind was devoted to His worship—
and Mayūkha, long bring delight to this great *Candrāloka* composed by the excellent poet Jayadeva, for [the chapters] are numbered as those of the sages (seven).
That sound which, when manifested, leads to the stilling of the mind is our *dhvani*;
otherwise, however, it results in the threefold *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya*.
In some cases, it is the manifestation itself that is suggested; in some cases, it is so by the very nature of the meaning;
and in some cases, it relinquishes its beauty before that which is more beautiful.
One should understand that the "unconcealed" (agūḍha) includes such figures as *arthāntarasaṃkramita* and so forth.
O Lord of Waters, have you forgotten Agastya, who was born from a water-jar?
If one *rasa* or the like is the subordinate element (*aṅga*) of another *rasa* or the like, [then there is subordination].
Alas, alas! My chest, smeared with saffron from my breasts, has been pierced by arrows.
Likewise, just as a boat is a means for accomplishing one's purpose across the ocean,
so do the wise, relying upon the raft of the teaching, cross over the oceans of disease.
In this case, it is considered that the breasts are indistinctly like the *kokas* bird;
my mind plunges into the pair of breasts anointed with saffron.
If there is doubt, let it be a doubt like that between the length of a lotus and [the length of] her eyes,
once those eyes have reached the position of ear-ornaments.
O beautiful one, the lotus, bearing a resemblance to your facial luster, undergoes a loss of splendor as if its status as the moon were equal in importance to that of your face.
If the suggested meaning were unpleasant—that is, less charming than the expressed meaning—it would be like this:
"The ruddy goose gazes at his beloved amidst the closing lotuses in the lake. (JCand_8.9)
"May the ocean bow down to the descendant of Kakutstha; today may Rāvaṇa rejoice!"—thus have the wise accepted the eightfold varieties of subordinate suggestion (*guṇībhūta-vyaṅgya*). 8.10.

May that eighth ray of the Sun, who is the Great God (Mahādeva) uniquely skilled in the science of sacrifices headed by the Sattra, and whose parents were Sumitrā— whose mind was devoted to his worship—
and Sukavi Jayadeva, long delight [the reader] in the great *Candrāloka*.

When the primary meaning is not intended to be expressed, and [the word] is connected [to another meaning] through conventional usage (rūḍhi) or a specific purpose (prayojana), whether in its earlier or later stages, that is considered indication (lakṣaṇā).
Based on whether the word whose own meaning is to be indicated is merged or not merged [with the primary sense], that indication (lakṣaṇā) is twofold;
it is further threefold according to the distinction between the accomplished, the to-be-accomplished, and the constituent of the to-be-accomplished.
The purpose is also twofold, distinguished as manifest and unmanifest;
the wise know the manifest to be further divided into two types: that which is peripheral and that which pertains to the object.

It is also twofold because it is either unmanifest (*asphuṭa*) due to being grounded in the meaning or because it is peripheral (*taṭastha*); furthermore, even that which is established in the meaning is twofold because it is grounded in either the object to be defined (*lakṣya*) or the defining characteristic (*lakṣaka*). (JCand 9.4)
Where it is clearly situated within the indicated object (*lakṣya*), that is the characteristic of the discerning (*vicakṣaṇa-lakṣaṇā*).
Its lack of clarity consists in being situated on the periphery (*taṭasthatva*) and its being situated within the indicated object (*lakṣyasthatva*). (JC 9.5)
"The other three are manifest from her power; thus she is fourfold.
She is indeed the moon, and her face is its orb; excellence is perceived in her countenance."
In the case of "Increase the lamp," the rise of auspiciousness is incidental;
however, in instances such as "This cloth is burnt," there is clearly no [such] purpose.
In such passages as "The nectar is well-spoken," the quality of being exceedingly heart-pleasing resides in the object of indication (*lakṣya*);
this is due to its being oriented toward [the subject], its proximity, and the perception of it in that very form. (JCand 9.8)
It arises from the relationship of cause and effect, from the relationship of the signified and the signifier,
and from other such relationships— namely, from these four.

Due to similarity, due to inherence, due to the opposite, and due to connection with action—there are two types each, the metaphorical (gauṇa) and the pure (śuddha), known as superimposition (sāropa) and identification (adhyavasāna). // JCand_9.10 //
The metaphorical *sāropā* (superimposition) is illustrated by such examples as "the moon is the face";
the metaphorical *sādhyavasānā* (resolution) would be such as "this is indeed the moon. JCand_9.11 //
The pure *sāropā* (superimposition) is taught as, for example, "Clarified butter is life"; the pure *sādhyavasānā* (identification) would be, for example, "This is indeed life."
There are two others by way of the offering of the substrate; thus, [the metaphor] is sixfold:
"The spears enter the Ganges" and "The hamlet dwells [in the river]. (JCand 9.13)
Furthermore, due to the distinction between the indicated and the indicator, [poetry] is of two kinds:
poetry with aesthetic flavor (sarasam kāvyam) is nectar, and knowledge is the most stable wealth.
Likewise, he was possessed of all causes [of excellence], yet in some respects he was distinguished by the absence of such [worldly] divisions;
in beauty he was Kandarpa himself, and she was Rati incarnate.
Whether in the word, the referent of the word, the sentence-meaning, number, grammatical relation, or gender,
this [suggestion] exists as the seed for the sprout of poetic ornament.

May that ninth ray [of the Sun] bring long-lasting joy to the *Candrāloka*, the great work composed by the excellent poet Jayadeva; he whose parents were Mahādeva—solely adept in the science of sacrifices headed by the *sattra*—and Sumitrā, whose mind was devoted to his worship.
A word generally functions by placing some property (dharma) in the foreground;
that function by which the word clearly expresses its object is known as denotation (abhidhā).
The wise declare that expression is of six kinds: by genus, by quality, by action, by connection with a substance, by name, and likewise by description. (JCand_10.2)

In sequence: "cow," "blue," "cook," "staff-bearer," "Ḍittha," and "Kaṃsa. [The word] "Kaṃsa" destroys "kaṃ" (pleasure); and the enemy of Kaṃsa (Kaṃsāri) [destroys] "kaṃ" (pleasure) which has taken refuge in man.
This term "description" does not have its locus in yoga or the like, nor is it a conventional abode; rather, it is used in its primary sense according to its own denotation.
O wise ones, having attained this moonlight that is enchanting, which originates from a shower of nectar, and which is a treasury of ambrosia, take refuge in joy!
Victorious are the words of the poet Jayadeva, born from the body of the illustrious Mahādeva, the sacrificial priest,
which rain down the nectar of eloquent verses.

May that tenth ray [of the moon] bring joy for a long time to the great *Candrāloka* composed by the excellent poet Jayadeva—[the moon] whose parents were Mahādeva, uniquely skilled in the science of sacrificial rites headed by the *Sattra*, and Sumitrā, whose mind was devoted to his worship. (JCand_10.7)
